Principles

Source: vignettes/articles/principles.Rmd
principles.Rmd

Every connection in GiottoConnect, whether a converter or an external tool, follows the same rules. They keep the package light to install, give credit to the people whose methods it runs, and let it work at any data size.

Dependencies

Only what every conversion needs is required. Seurat, anndataR, SpatialExperiment and every external tool are optional. Each function checks for the packages it uses when it runs, and says how to install them.

No python for conversions. Seurat, AnnData and SpatialExperiment conversions run in R; .h5ad files are read and written without python. Python tools run through reticulate, which installs them into a managed environment the first time they run. Conda is never needed.

Credit

Every external tool cites its paper, in three places:

  • its help page lists the paper and asks users to cite it;
  • the citation is printed the first time the tool runs in a session;
  • objCitations() lists the papers of every method used on an object, also for an object saved with saveGiotto().
g <- runBanksy(g)
#> If you use runBanksy() in published research, please cite:
#>   Singhal V, Chou N, Lee J, et al. (2024). "BANKSY unifies cell typing and
#>   tissue domain segmentation for scalable spatial omics data analysis."
#>   Nature Genetics, 56, 431-441. doi:10.1038/s41588-024-01664-3.

objCitations(g)

options(giotto.cite = FALSE) turns the messages off.

Design

Wrap, never reimplement. GiottoConnect runs the original implementation of a method. When the Suite has its own implementation of a method, it lives in Giotto, not here.

One pattern for every tool. A tool is a param class holding its settings, a method that runs it on a matrix, and a run<Tool>() function that takes a giotto object, runs the method and stores the results. The param is recorded in the object’s history, so objHistory() shows how a result was made.

No version names. There is one seuratToGiotto(), not one per Seurat version. When an object’s structure changes, GiottoConnect gets a new mapping file; the function stays the same.

Nothing is lost silently. What a conversion cannot carry over is reported when it runs and listed by mappingProvenance().

Scale

Everything works on disk-backed objects. Converters can write straight into a GiottoDisk project (source =), streaming large matrices instead of loading them into memory. Tools read their input only through Giotto’s accessors and verbs, never from the object’s slots, so the same code can serve in-memory and disk-backed objects.

Adding a tool

A new tool follows the pattern of the existing ones (for example R/tool-nnsvg.R in the package source), in a file of its own:

  1. A <tool>Param() constructor and class, with a methodCitation() method returning the paper as a utils::bibentry().
  2. A method on one of GiottoClass’s analysis verbs (analyzeData(), reduceData(), clusterData(), …) that runs the tool on a matrix.
  3. run<Tool>(), which reads from the giotto object, calls the method, stores the results with the setters and records the param: update_giotto_params(gobject, description = "_<tool>", attachments = list(param = param)).
  4. A help page with the paper under References.
  5. A test that runs checkGiottoMethod() on the result. It checks that only the declared slots changed, that results cover every cell, that the param is in the history with a citation, and that the help page cites the paper.
g2 <- runMyTool(g)
checkGiottoMethod(g, g2, slots = "cell_metadata",
    param_class = "myToolParam", fn = "runMyTool", package = "GiottoConnect")
